p.src: As they journeyed on, evening fell before they knew it. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, it is growing late again. Where shall we spend the night?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, that is not the right thing to say. Those who have left the world dine on wind and lodge by water, lie beneath the moon and sleep amid frost; wherever they are is home. Why ask where we are to rest?” Zhu Bajie said, “Brother, you travel light and easy, so how would you care how burdened and weary others are? Ever since we crossed the River of Flowing Sands, we have been climbing mountains and crossing ridges all this while, and I have had to carry this heavy load. It is more than I can bear. We ought to find a household where, first, we can beg some tea and food and, second, recover our strength. That would make sense.” The Pilgrim said, “Idiot, those words of yours sound rather like a grievance. You may wish for the idle, carefree life you enjoyed at Gao Village, seeking no merit, but I fear that is no longer possible. p.src: With so much luggage, it is hard on old Zhu to carry it alone day after day. You get to be Master’s disciple, while you treat me like a hired hand.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Idiot, whom are you saying this to?” Bajie said, “I am saying it to you, brother.” The Pilgrim said, “Then you have complained to the wrong person. Old Sun is responsible only for Master’s safety; you and Sha Monk are charged especially with the luggage and the horse. If you neglect them in the least, the first thing you will get is a sound cudgeling on the shins.” Bajie said, “Brother, do not speak of beating me. Beating someone is using strength to bully him. I know how proud and lofty your noble nature is; you certainly will not agree to carry anything. But the horse Master rides is so tall and well fed, and carries only the old monk. Letting it take a few pieces would at least show some brotherly feeling.”

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “You call him a horse, but he is no ordinary horse. He was originally a son of Ao Run, Dragon King of the Western Sea, and was called the Third Dragon Prince. Because he set fire to a bright pearl in the palace, his father accused him of unfilial rebellion. He violated the laws of Heaven and owed his life entirely to the intervention of the Bodhisattva Guanyin. He waited a long time for Master in the steep torrent of Eagle-Grief, and fortunately the Bodhisattva came in person, stripped off his scales and horns, and removed the pearl beneath his neck. Only then was he transformed into this horse, and he vowed to carry Master to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha. These are the merits and destined fruits allotted to each of us. Do not try to drag him into your burden.” When Sha Monk heard this, he asked, “Brother, is he truly a dragon?” The Pilgrim said, “He is a dragon.” Bajie said, “Brother, I have heard the ancients say that dragons can breathe out clouds and belch forth mist, scatter earth and raise sand; they possess the power to shoulder mountains and wrench apart ridges, and the magic to overturn rivers and churn the seas. Why, then, does he amble along so slowly today?” The Pilgrim said, “If you want him to go fast, I shall make him go fast and let you see.”

The master’s hands were weak, and he could not rein it in. The horse ran wild until it reached a mountain cliff, where at last it slowed to an unsteady walk. p.src: As the master held the reins and slowly surveyed the scene, Wukong and his brothers finally arrived. Wujing asked, “Master, you did not fall from the horse, did you?” The elder scolded him: “That accursed ape Wukong startled the horse! It was fortunate indeed that I managed to stay in the saddle.” The Pilgrim smiled apologetically and said, “Master, do not scold me. Zhu Bajie said the horse was too slow, so I merely made it go a little faster.” The idiot had hurried in pursuit of the horse and now panted heavily. Muttering and grumbling, he made a commotion: “Enough, enough! Everyone looks after his own belly and lets another’s belt hang loose. The load is so heavy I can hardly shoulder it, yet you make me run about chasing the horse as well.” The elder said, “Disciples, look: there is a manor over there. We can go and ask to lodge for the night.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim hurriedly raised his head and looked. Sure enough, auspicious clouds canopied the place high in the air, and blessed vapors filled and veiled it. He knew at once that it must be a manifestation conjured by a Buddha or an immortal, but dared not divulge Heaven’s secret. He merely said, “Good, good, good! Let us go and ask for lodging.”

p.src: The elder hurriedly dismounted. Before them stood a gatehouse with pendant-lotus and elephant-trunk brackets, painted rafters, and carved beams. Sha Monk set down the luggage, and Bajie, holding the horse, said, “This household is a truly wealthy and substantial one.” The Pilgrim was about to enter, but Tripitaka said, “You must not. As men who have left the world, you and I must be careful to avoid suspicion. We must on no account enter uninvited. Let us wait until someone comes out, and then courteously ask for lodging. Only then may we enter.” Bajie tethered the horse and leaned against the foot of the wall; Tripitaka sat upon a stone drum; and the Pilgrim and Sha Monk sat at the edge of the raised platform. When no one emerged for a long while, the impatient Pilgrim sprang up and went through the gate to look. Inside he found a great south-facing hall of three bays, with its latticed curtains raised high. On the screen door hung a horizontal painting depicting a Mountain of Longevity and a Sea of Blessings; and on the two gold-lacquered pillars was pasted a pair of spring couplets on bright red paper. The first read: “Silken strands drift from tender willows by the level bridge at dusk; Snowflakes speckle fragrant plum blossoms in the little courtyard in spring.” In the center stood a dark, softly polished black-lacquer incense table, upon which rested an antique bronze censer shaped like a beast. There were six armchairs, while four hanging panels depicting the seasons adorned the walls at either end.

p.src: While the Pilgrim was secretly peering about, he suddenly heard footsteps behind the rear door. A woman of indeterminate middle age came out and asked in a sweet voice, “Who are you, to enter a widow’s house without permission?” The Great Sage was so startled that he bowed and answered with repeated assent: “This humble monk has come from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, bearing an imperial command to journey west, worship the Buddha, and seek the scriptures. Our company of four happened to pass through your honored region, and as night has fallen, we have come especially to your venerable residence to beg lodging for one night.” The woman greeted him with a smile and said, “Elder, where are the other three? Please bring them in.” The Pilgrim called loudly, “Master, please come in!” Only then did Tripitaka enter with Bajie and Sha Monk, leading the horse and carrying the luggage, while the woman came out of the hall to welcome them. Bajie narrowed his eyes and stole a glance at her. And how, you may ask, was she attired?

p.src: When the woman saw the three disciples, she was more delighted than ever and courteously invited them into the hall. After they had exchanged greetings one by one, she invited them to take their seats and served tea. Suddenly, from behind the screen came a young maid with looped hair and trailing tresses, bearing a golden tray and white-jade cups; the fragrant tea breathed warm steam, while rare fruits diffused a delicate perfume. She drew back her colored sleeves, revealing fingers slender as spring bamboo shoots; raising the jade cups, she passed the tea and offered it to them. She bowed to each of them in turn. When tea was finished, the woman ordered a vegetarian meal to be prepared. Tripitaka raised his hands in greeting and said, “Venerable lady, what is your honored surname? And what is this place called?” The woman replied, “This region lies in the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift. My maiden surname is Jia, and my husband’s family name was Mo. When I was young, misfortune struck: my parents-in-law died early, and my husband and I were left to maintain the ancestral estate. We possessed a fortune worth ten thousand strings of cash and a thousand qing of fertile land. Yet husband and wife were fated to have no son, and we had only three daughters. Then, most unhappily, my husband too died the year before last. I have lived as a widow, and this year my mourning period ended. All that remains is the land and family estate. We have no other kin or relations, so my daughters and I alone must inherit it. I would marry again, but I cannot bear to abandon the estate. Now that you venerable monks have graciously descended upon us, I see that master and disciples number four, while my daughters and I are four women. We wish to remain here and take husbands into the household; the four of you would suit us exactly. I wonder whether this proposal meets with your honored approval?” Hearing this, Tripitaka pretended to be deaf and dumb, closed his eyes, composed his mind, and answered not a word.

p.src: The woman continued, “Our household owns more than three hundred qing of paddy fields, more than three hundred qing of dry fields, and more than three hundred qing of mountain orchards; we have over a thousand yellow water buffalo, herds of mules and horses, and pigs and sheep beyond number; in every direction—east, south, west, and north—we own some sixty or seventy manors, forts, and grazing grounds; at home there is enough rice and grain to go unused for eight or nine years, enough damask and silk to remain unworn for a decade, and enough gold and silver to last a lifetime without being spent. This far surpasses hiding springtime delights behind embroidered curtains—why even speak of two rows of golden hairpins? If you master and disciples would only change your minds and marry into my humble household, you could live at ease and enjoy wealth and honor. Would that not be far better than wearing yourselves out on the journey west?” But Tripitaka merely sat there as though witless and dull, saying nothing.

p.src: The woman said, “I was born at the hour of the Rooster on the third day of the third month in a dinghai year. My late husband was three years older than I, and I am forty-five this year. My eldest daughter is named Zhenzhen and is twenty this year; my second daughter is named Aiai and is eighteen; and my youngest daughter is named Lianlian and is sixteen. None has yet been betrothed. Though I myself am homely, fortunately all three girls possess some beauty, and there is no kind of women’s work or needlecraft they cannot do. Since my late husband had no son, we raised them as sons. When they were young, they were taught to read some Confucian books, and all know something of composing verse and matching couplets. Though they live in a country manor, they are by no means coarse or vulgar. I daresay they are worthy matches for you reverend gentlemen. If you would only open your hearts, let your hair grow, and become heads of our household, you could dress in silk and brocade. Surely that would be better than your earthen bowls, black robes, straw sandals, and cloud hats.” Seated above them, Tripitaka looked just like a child stunned by thunder or a toad drenched in rain: he sat rigid and dazed, rolling up the whites of his eyes and leaning backward.

p.src: When Bajie heard of such wealth and such beauty, his heart began to itch beyond endurance; sitting on his chair, he twisted this way and that as if needles were pricking his backside, unable to contain himself. He stepped forward, tugged at his master, and said, “Master, this lady is speaking to you. Why do you pretend not to notice? You ought at least to give her some sort of answer.” The master suddenly raised his head and, with a sharp cry, shouted Bajie back: “You sinful beast! We are men who have left the household life. How could we let riches and honor stir our hearts or set our minds on feminine beauty? What principle would there be in that?”

p.src: Hearing this, the woman flew into a rage and cried, “What an insolent rogue of a monk! Were it not that you have come from far away in the Eastern Land, I would have you driven out at once. I sincerely meant to offer my family estate and take you all as sons-in-law, yet you repay me with wounding words. Even if you yourself have taken vows and sworn never to return to secular life, surely my family might take one of your disciples. Why must you cling so rigidly to the rules?” Seeing her anger, Tripitaka could only stammer apologetically, “Wukong, you remain here, then.” Pilgrim replied, “I have never understood how to do such things, not since I was little. Let Bajie remain here.” Bajie said, “Brother, don’t frame me! We should all take our time and discuss this properly.” Tripitaka said, “If neither of you is willing, then let Wujing remain here.” Friar Sand said, “Just listen to what Master is saying! Through the Bodhisattva’s exhortation and conversion, your disciple accepted the precepts and waited for Master. Since Master took me in, I have received your instruction and followed you for not yet two months, but I have not earned even the slightest merit. How could I dare covet such wealth and honor? I would rather die than fail to go to the Western Heaven; I will never do a deed that betrays my own conscience.”

p.src: When the woman saw that they all refused, she abruptly turned and went behind the screen, then slammed the inner door shut. Master and disciples were abandoned outside without tea or food, and no one came out again. Bajie grew anxious and irritable, and complained to the Tang Monk, “Master, you truly don’t know how to handle affairs. You spoke so absolutely that you killed off every possibility. You ought to have left yourself some room, answered her vaguely, and coaxed a vegetarian meal out of her. Then at least we could have passed tonight in comfort. Tomorrow, whether we agreed or refused would still have been up to us. Now that they have shut the door and refuse to come out, how are we to pass the night beside this cold, ashen stove?”

Master and disciples were abandoned outside without tea or food, and no one came out again.
Bajie grew anxious and irritable, and complained to the Tang Monk, “Master, you truly don’t know how to handle affairs. You spoke so absolutely that you killed off every possibility.
You ought to have left yourself some room, answered her vaguely, and coaxed a vegetarian meal out of her. Then at least we could have passed tonight in comfort.
Tomorrow, whether we agreed or refused would still have been up to us.
Now that they have shut the door and refuse to come out, how are we to pass the night beside this cold, ashen stove?”

p.src: Wujing said, “Second Brother, why not become a son-in-law in this household?” Bajie said, “Brother, don’t set me up. Let’s think it over carefully.” The Pilgrim said, “What is there to think over? If you are willing, we’ll have Master and the lady become in-laws, and you can marry into her household as a resident son-in-law. Her family is so rich in money and treasure that they will surely provide a handsome dowry and prepare a feast for the new relatives. We too will enjoy some of it, while you return to lay life and remain here. Would that not satisfy both sides perfectly?” Bajie said, “That may be true, but I left the world only to return to it, and abandoned one wife only to marry another.” Monk Sha said, “So you already have a wife, Second Brother?” The Pilgrim said, “You still do not know his story. He was once the son-in-law of Squire Gao at Old Gao’s Village in the land of Wusizang, until I subdued him. He had also accepted the Bodhisattva’s precepts. With no other choice, I seized him and made him a monk; thus he left his former wife and followed Master westward to worship the Buddha. He must have been parted from her so long that he began thinking of that business again; and the moment he heard of this present opportunity, the desire naturally returned. You fool, become this family’s son-in-law. Just bow to me a few more times, and I will refrain from reporting you.” The fool said, “Nonsense! Nonsense! p.src: The fool led the horse along, refusing to let it graze even where there was grass. Clicking and shooing at it, he drove it around to the rear gate. p.src: Before long, they saw the fool return with the horse and tether it. The elder asked, “Did you graze the horse?” Bajie said, “There was no good grass and nowhere to graze it.” The Pilgrim said, “Nowhere to graze the horse—but was there somewhere to lead it?” Hearing this, the fool knew his secret had leaked. He hung his head, twisted his neck, pursed his lips, and furrowed his brow, saying nothing for a long while. Then came a creak as the inner gate opened. p.src: Tripitaka joined his palms and lowered his head; the Great Sage Sun pretended not to notice them; and Monk Sha turned his back. But Zhu Bajie stared without blinking. His lustful thoughts ran wild and his lecherous courage swelled; mincing forward, he whispered, “Thank you, fair immortals, for descending among us. Mother, please ask the elder sisters to go in.” The three young women withdrew behind the screen, leaving behind a pair of gauze lanterns. The lady said, “Have you four reverends given the matter thought? Which one of you will marry my daughter?” Wujing said, “We have already discussed it. The one surnamed Zhu shall marry into your household.” Bajie said, “Brother, don’t set me up. Let everyone discuss it together.” The Pilgrim said, “What is left to discuss? You settled everything perfectly at the rear gate and have already called her ‘Mother.’ What more is there to discuss? Master shall represent the groom’s family, this old lady the bride’s; I shall act as guarantor, and Monk Sha as matchmaker. There is no need even to consult the almanac. Today is a most auspicious day blessed by Heaven. Bow to Master and go inside to become the son-in-law.” Bajie said, “It won’t do, it won’t do! How could I possibly go through with such a business?” The Pilgrim said, “Fool, stop making a fuss. Who knows how many times you called her ‘Mother’? How can you now say it will not do? Agree at once, and let us share some wedding wine. That will be a benefit to us too.” With one hand he seized Bajie and with the other he pulled the lady toward him, saying, “Dear mother-in-law, take your son-in-law inside.” The fool’s feet shuffled sideways as he tried to go with her. The lady immediately called to the servants, “Wipe and set out the tables and chairs, prepare the evening vegetarian meal, and entertain the three honored in-laws. I shall take the bridegroom to the inner rooms.” At the same time, she ordered the cooks to prepare a banquet for the meeting of the relatives the next morning. The servants received their orders. The other three ate their vegetarian meal, hastily spread their bedding, and settled down in the guest chamber. Of them we shall say no more for now.

p.src: Now Bajie followed his mother-in-law inside. They passed through layer upon layer of buildings—he could not tell how many—and he stumbled and bumped along, tripping over thresholds everywhere. The fool said, “Mother, walk a little slower. I don’t know my way in here—please lead me by the hand.” The woman said, “These are all granaries, storehouses, milling rooms, and the like. We haven’t even reached the kitchens yet.” “What an enormous household!” said Bajie. Stumbling and bumping, turning corner after corner, they walked for quite a while longer before at last reaching the inner hall and chambers. The woman said, “Son-in-law, your senior brother said that today is a most auspicious day blessed by Heaven, so I have brought you in to marry. But everything was so hurried that we had no time to invite a diviner or perform the wedding rites and prepare the bridal bed. Just bow eight times toward the place of honor.” Bajie said, “You are quite right, Mother. Please take the seat of honor and let me bow to you several times. It can count both as the wedding ceremony and as thanks to my new kin—two things done at once. Wouldn’t that save trouble?” His mother-in-law laughed. “Very well, very well. You truly are a capable son-in-law who knows how to run a household economically. I shall sit, and you may bow.”

p.src: Ah! Silver candles shone brilliantly throughout the hall as the fool bowed toward the seat of honor. When he had finished, he asked, “Mother, which of the elder sisters will you give me as my wife?” His mother-in-law said, “That is precisely the difficulty. If I give you my eldest daughter, I fear the second will complain; if I give you the second, I fear the third will complain; and if I give you the third, I fear the eldest will complain. That is why I still cannot decide.” Bajie said, “Mother, if you fear they will quarrel, give them all to me. That will spare us noisy squabbling and keep the household rules from being thrown into disorder.” His mother-in-law said, “What an absurd idea! Would you monopolize all three of my daughters by yourself?” Bajie said, “Listen to what you are saying, Mother. What man does not have three or four wives and concubines? Even if there were several more, your son-in-law would gladly accept them. In my youth I learned the art of battling through the night, and I guarantee I can attend to each of them to her full satisfaction.” The woman said, “No, no. I have a handkerchief here. Put it over your head to cover your face, and let Heaven choose your bride. I shall have my daughters walk past you; whichever one you catch when you reach out shall be given to you as your wife.” The fool agreed, took the handkerchief, and draped it over his head. p.src: When the fool had arranged the covering properly, he said, “Mother, ask the sisters to come out.” His mother-in-law called, “Zhenzhen, Aiai, Lianlian, come and let Heaven choose which of you shall wed your husband!” There came only the clear chiming of girdle pendants and the fragrance of orchids and musk, as though immortal maidens were passing to and fro. The fool truly stretched out his hands to grab someone, lunging wildly from side to side, but he caught no one on the left and no one on the right. They came and went; he could not tell how many women were moving around him, yet he had no hope of catching even one. Lunging east, he embraced a pillar; lunging west, he felt a wooden wall. Dashing back and forth made him so dizzy that he could not stand steady and kept tumbling over. He kicked a door panel going forward and crashed into a brick wall going back. Battered and bruised, with swollen lips and a blue forehead, he fell sitting on the ground. Panting heavily, he said, “Mother! Your daughters are far too sly. I cannot catch a single one. What am I to do? What am I to do?”

p.src: The woman removed his veil and said, “Son-in-law, it is not that my daughters are sly. Each is yielding to the others and unwilling to take you as her husband.” Bajie said, “Mother, if they will not take me, then you take me yourself.” The woman said, “Fine son-in-law you are! Have you no sense of rank or propriety, that you even want your own mother-in-law?” My three daughters are exceptionally ingenious. Each has knotted a pearl-studded brocade undershirt. Whichever one fits you shall be the one to take you as her husband.” Bajie said, “Good, good, good! Bring all three for me to try. If they all fit, let all three take me as their husband.” The woman went into the room but brought out only one garment, which she handed to Bajie. The fool took off his blue brocade robe, accepted the undershirt, and put it on. Before he had even fastened the sash, he was jerked off his feet with a thump and fell to the ground. It turned out that several cords had drawn tight around him. The fool could scarcely endure the pain, while all those people had already vanished.
